title: SCOR and AXA XL Back Ecological Restoration Insurance Through Lloyd's, With SCOR's Syndicate 2015 Leading the 'Restore' Product
summary: SCOR and AXA announced in January 2026 a Lloyd's consortium to insure the implementation phase of ecological restoration projects, led by SCOR's Syndicate 2015 with AXA XL's Syndicate 2003 in support, as part of SCOR's NatReCo nature initiative.
description:
Two of Europe's largest risk carriers have joined forces at Lloyd's to insure nature restoration. SCOR, the French reinsurer, and AXA, the French insurer, announced on January 20 and 21, 2026 that they had formed a consortium at Lloyd's of London to underwrite ecological restoration projects. The reports reviewed here say that SCOR's Syndicate 2015, run by SCOR Managing Agency Ltd, leads the consortium and that AXA XL's Syndicate 2003 supports it. Earlier coverage of this story placed it in July, but the announcement dates from January 2026.

What the consortium actually insures is described narrowly. It underwrites SCOR's product called Restore, which covers the implementation phase of an ecological restoration project. That is the stage in which the work is done, such as planting, rewetting land or rebuilding habitat, as opposed to the years afterwards in which the ecosystem is expected to recover and deliver benefits. The distinction matters because the construction stage is where capital is spent and where physical events can destroy the work before it matures. A fire, a flood or a storm during implementation can wipe out the investment, and the lack of cover for that risk is one reason private investors have been cautious.

The consortium is part of a wider SCOR programme. In May 2024, the group launched an initiative called NatReCo, which stands for nature restoration and conservation, to develop insurance and reinsurance solutions that support nature. Restore is the product built under that banner. According to the coverage, the aim is to bring insurance capacity, expertise and risk modelling to a field that has relied mostly on grants and philanthropic funding.

Quotes from the participants show how they frame the move. Jean-Paul Conoscente, chief executive of SCOR's property and casualty business, and Henry Mumme-Young of SCOR spoke about using Lloyd's as a platform for innovation, while Etienne Champion, chief underwriting officer for AXA's property and casualty commercial group, said the partnership reflects AXA's commitment to supporting restoration. These are company statements and describe intent rather than results.

The scale and structure of the cover are not disclosed. The announcements gave no capacity figure, so it is not known how much risk the consortium can take on, and they named no projects or clients. They also did not describe the product as parametric, meaning one that pays out when a predefined index is hit rather than after a loss assessment, so readers should not assume that structure. Pricing, deductibles and exclusions were not reported either.

The economic argument for the product comes from the statistics that SCOR and AXA used. They cite that roughly half of the world economy depends on healthy ecosystems and that the World Economic Forum ranks biodiversity loss as the second most severe environmental risk over a ten-year horizon. The logic is that if nature underpins so much economic activity, restoring it has value, and if investors are to fund restoration, they need risk transfer that is similar to what they expect in infrastructure or agriculture.

There are reasons for caution. Restoration is long term, and outcomes depend on ecology as much as on engineering. Insurance for the implementation phase protects against damage during the work, but it does not guarantee that the ecosystem will recover or that biodiversity targets will be met. Insurers will therefore need clear definitions of what is covered, good data on site conditions and monitoring that is trusted by both investors and underwriters. A new product also has no loss history, so initial pricing will rely on modelling and judgment.

For the market, the significance is that two large groups see nature restoration as an underwriting opportunity, not only as a topic for sustainability reports. If the product works, it could be copied by other Lloyd's syndicates and carriers, and it could make restoration projects bankable for lenders that currently decline them. Developers and landowners considering restoration should ask what perils are covered during implementation, how the policy treats events that are partly caused by poor site management, and whether cover extends beyond the first phase.

What to watch next is the first disclosed projects and any information on capacity. If SCOR and AXA publish case studies or loss data, the market will learn whether this is a niche product or the start of a larger line of business. For now, the verified facts are limited to who leads, what is covered and which programme it belongs to.

It also helps to understand why restoration is hard to finance. A reforestation or wetland project can take years to deliver measurable benefits, and its revenue, if any, often depends on credits, grants or payments linked to outcomes. Lenders look for a clear route to repayment and a way to limit loss if something goes wrong in the early years. Insurance cannot supply the revenue, but it can reduce the chance that an unexpected event ends the project before it starts. That is the gap Restore is intended to fill, according to the way the companies describe it.

Lloyd's is a natural place for the product because of how it works. Syndicates at Lloyd's compete to write specialist risks, and a consortium lets more than one syndicate share a new line while it is being established. Having both SCOR and AXA XL involved gives the product two sources of underwriting expertise and signals to brokers that the market is serious. The reports do not say whether other syndicates may join, or how the lead underwriter will set terms for each project, which are details that brokers and developers will want to see.

Readers should keep the scope in mind. This is an insurance product for the work phase of restoration, announced by the companies, with no published volumes. It is not a guarantee that nature restoration will be funded at scale, and it will take real projects and claims experience before its value can be judged.

key_points: SCOR and AXA announced the Lloyd's consortium on January 20 to 21, 2026, with SCOR Syndicate 2015 leading and AXA XL Syndicate 2003 supporting.
The consortium underwrites SCOR's 'Restore' product, which covers the implementation phase of ecological restoration projects.
It sits inside SCOR's NatReCo initiative, launched in May 2024, to build insurance and reinsurance solutions for nature.
The announcements gave no capacity figure and no named projects, and did not describe the cover as parametric.
SCOR and AXA cite roughly half of the world economy as dependent on healthy ecosystems, and the World Economic Forum ranks biodiversity loss second among environmental risks over ten years.
why_it_matters: Restoration projects need private money, and investors want to know that a failed planting or a storm will not wipe out their capital. Insurance that covers the building phase can make such projects easier to finance, but the product is new and its limits will only become clear as policies are written.
